entries.name: Curtis Lab
entries.focus: The lab treats cancer as an evolving ecosystem. It quantifies and forecasts tumour evolutionary dynamics and maps genotype to phenotype in malignancy. Methods include AI/ML and agent-based models, along with dynamic 'world' models and digital twins built from longitudinal patient cohorts. It integrates multi-modal data (genomics, transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, glycomics, digital pathology) from patient cohorts and clinical trials. Experimental work uses patient-derived organoids and organ-on-a-chip systems, plus robotic high-throughput perturbation. The lab also designs computational immunotherapies and biomarkers for early detection and treatment decisions.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with cancer genomics, computational/ML methods and spatial/single-cell omics, and tumour evolution from sequencing is a natural match for Marra Lab work. The lab is less focused on structural variants and WGS or transcriptome methods specifically, and a US role would need a visa.

flags: PI is still at Stanford; no move found. The old Stanford lab page (med.stanford.edu/curtislab.html) says the lab has moved to curtis-lab.com, and the old team.html URL returned 404.
The people page lists the students as 'Graduate Student' without saying PhD. I treated them as PhD students, but the list may include non-PhD trainees.
No years or emails are published on the people page.
The people page also lists four clinical fellows (Marni McClure, Audris Chiang, Colin Bergstrom, Zach Ziheng Xu). I excluded them as non-postdocs.
I did not verify the PI's Google Scholar URL, so it is null.

entries.name: Goodarzi Lab
entries.focus: The lab combines experimental and computational genomics to study how RNA-encoded gene regulation is altered in human disease, especially cancer. entries.name: Van Loo Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how tumours evolve, using what it calls the "molecular archeology of cancer" to reconstruct the evolutionary history and subclonal structure of tumours. It asks how cancers develop and progress, how metastasis spreads, and how resistance to therapy emerges. The main method is massively parallel (whole-genome) sequencing. Work includes large pan-cancer studies and focused studies of specific tumour types, such as gastrointestinal, pancreatic, colorectal and sarcoma cancers. The lab also looks at genome evolution, epigenetics and DNA methylation, and it builds computational methods for copy-number, clonality and mutation-timing analysis.

fit.reason: The lab's work on tumour WGS, somatic mutation and copy-number analysis, and computational method development matches the student's cancer genomics and somatic-variant interests closely. Single-cell and spatial omics is not a stated focus.

entries.name: Alexandrov Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops machine-learning and computational methods to study the molecular mechanisms of cancer development and progression. A core theme is mutational signatures: the SigProfiler tool suite is used to find the mutational footprints of endogenous and exogenous processes in cancer and normal genomes. Related work covers copy-number and structural signatures, APOBEC mutagenesis, and microbial exposures such as colibactin in early-onset colorectal cancer. The lab also uses high-accuracy duplex sequencing of normal tissues to study somatic mutation, aging and cancer predisposition. It also applies deep learning to histopathology slides and works on genomic biomarkers of treatment response.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interests in somatic mutation and structural-variant analysis, cancer whole-genome sequencing and ML for genomics. Single-cell and spatial omics is the only minor gap, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Getz Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies cancer genomes. It looks at somatic events that drive cancer or resistance, and at germline variants that affect cancer risk. It relates these to disease subtypes, clinical features and treatment outcomes. Its work has two stages. First, it characterizes the DNA, RNA and protein changes in an individual patient's tumour compared with normal tissue. Second, it interprets those changes across patient cohorts to find genes, pathways and molecular subtypes. The lab builds and maintains widely used analysis tools and pipelines for national and international cancer genome projects, such as mutation, copy-number and significance-of-mutation analysis. It also studies the tumour and its immune microenvironment with bulk and single-cell RNA-seq, and its members work on spatial omics and other computational methods. The lab's own site does not describe its methods in more detail, so

fit.reason: The lab's core work is tumour genome and transcriptome analysis, somatic mutation and structural variant calling, and computational methods and single-cell/spatial work in cancer, which covers nearly all of the student's interests. The main drawback is that US roles would need a visa.

entries.name: Ding Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops and applies computational tools and experimental approaches to study cancer. It works with large multi-omic datasets, including genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic and proteogenomic data. The lab's cancer focus includes pancreatic, prostate, liver and gastrointestinal cancers.

entries.name: Ideker Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds AI-driven, mechanistic models of cancer and neurodegenerative disease that turn patient data into more precise diagnosis and treatment. A main thread is mapping subcellular networks and structures, including the Cancer Cell Map Initiative. Another is interpretable ('visible') machine learning, where neural networks are built to follow the hierarchy of cell biology so that predictions in predictive oncology can be explained. Other areas are network biomarkers for cancer and neuropsychiatric disease, epigenetic aging, and bioinformatics software such as Cytoscape and NDEx.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps on cancer genomics and computational/ML methods for genomics. It has little focus on whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and a US or UK role would need a visa.

entries.name: Palotie Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the genetic basis of common diseases using clinical and population samples from the Finnish founder population. entries.name: Klein Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how cells choose fates during development, regeneration and disease. It builds time-resolved single-cell maps of differentiation in zebrafish embryos, human airway epithelium and intestinal organoids, and it uses lineage tracing to link cell state to fate. It develops technologies including the inDrop droplet-barcoding platform and CAGE semi-permeable core-shell capsules, which support multi-step single-cell genomics, live-culture screens and cell-cell interaction mapping. Computational work includes algorithms for lineage-resolved trajectories, noise quantification, and predictive models of tissue behaviour. The lab also does functional genomics in bacteria and comparative immune evolution in Ciona. It does not work on cancer genomics.

entries.focus: The lab uses large-scale genomic and transcriptomic data to improve rare disease diagnosis through better rare variant interpretation and discovery of new disease genes. entries.name: Berger Lab
entries.focus: The lab is an interdisciplinary group in computer science, mathematics and biology. It builds machine learning, algorithmic and statistical tools for biological discovery and medicine. Current themes include large language models for biological sequences, machine learning for structural biology and protein design, and uncertainty estimation and calibration. Other themes are privacy-preserving and fair genomic analytics, algorithmic genomics, and causal inference and representation learning for single-cell data. Earlier work covered network biology and population genetics.

fit.reason: The lab's strengths in computational and ML methods for genomics and in single-cell analysis match the student's methods interests, but it does little cancer-specific work, tumour WGS or structural-variant calling, and the student would need a US visa.

entries.name: Uhler Lab
entries.department_hint: Core Institute Member; Eric and Wendy Schmidt Center
entries.focus: The group develops machine learning and statistical methods that integrate and translate between data types such as transcriptomic, proteomic and imaging data. It works on causal inference and causal representation learning, and on inferring regulatory relationships. A major theme is modelling single-cell perturbation data (for example, predicting the effects of genetic or chemical perturbations). A second theme is how 3D genome packing relates to gene regulation in health and disease. Much of the work is done with Broad experimental collaborators (Blainey, Chen, Van Allen, Xavier, Hacohen and others), and the group's focus is methods rather than cancer-specific sequencing analysis.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps with the student's interests in ML methods for genomics and single-cell/spatial omics (and has a Van Allen cancer co-advised postdoc), but its work is mostly causal ML and perturbation modelling rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis.

entries.focus: The lab develops machine learning and computational methods for small-molecule discovery and chemical synthesis. Work includes computer-aided synthesis planning and retrosynthesis, reaction outcome and mechanism prediction, and data-driven reaction optimization with automation and high-throughput experimentation. The lab does not do genomics or sequencing-based work.

entries.name: Neafsey Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies vector-borne disease, mainly malaria. It combines genomic, transcriptomic and serologic data on the parasites (Plasmodium falciparum and P. vivax), their Anopheles mosquito vectors and human hosts. Methods include whole-genome sequencing of parasites and mosquitoes, and low-cost multiplexed PCR amplicon sequencing developed for research and public-health surveillance. Population genomic and bioinformatic methods, especially identity-by-descent relatedness analysis, are used to infer transmission, migration, drug-resistance selection and fitness tradeoffs. The lab also runs molecular surveillance projects (for example in Guyana and Colombia) and distributes its pipelines on the Terra.bio cloud platform.

fit.reason: The lab has strong computational genomics and variant/selection analysis, but it works on malaria and mosquitoes rather than cancer, tumour sequencing, somatic or structural variants, or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.focus: The lab builds computational and experimental methods for biology and therapeutics, using interpretable models that are checked against experimental evidence. entries.focus: The lab's stated mission is 'machine learning to accelerate biology'. One thread learns the 'language of life' from patterns of co-evolving amino acids, which it uses to infer protein and RNA structure and function. A second thread predicts the effects of single and combined mutations. This is used to interpret human genetic variation and to design stable, functional proteins. A third thread uses machine learning on viral evolution and immunology to predict viral escape and pathogenicity, improve immune recognition and find antibody targets. Current members also work on T-cell receptor and immune-repertoire models, enzyme design, and cancer-focused ML in a joint postdoc position with Chris Sander.

It develops quantitative, scalable inference methods and models for somatic evolution in cancer, with an emphasis on the rapidly evolving genomes of tumours. The data it works with are single-cell genomic data and in situ imaging (spatial) data. The PI's earlier work was at MSK and Columbia, with a PhD from Cambridge and the Wellcome Sanger Institute. I could not read the lab's own page in full, so this description comes from snippets and the GitHub-hosted mirror.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's computational/ML methods, single-cell and spatial omics in cancer, and somatic mutation and genome evolution interests; there is less emphasis on bulk WGS/transcriptome and SV calling, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.name: Korsunsky Lab
entries.focus: The lab does computational biology on single-cell and spatial genomics data from human inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases. One strand builds algorithms and software that integrate genomic datasets across studies, donors and tissues. A second strand maps spatial gene and protein data to reconstruct tissue structure. A third models temporal dynamics of single-cell states to predict what drives pathogenic ones. A fourth compares diseases to find shared cell states or tissue-specific cell types. The PI's publications cover synovial fibroblasts in rheumatoid arthritis, including Notch signalling and adipocyte-associated glucocorticoid signalling.

fit.reason: The lab's single-cell and spatial omics methods and ML/computational genomics work match the student's methods interests, but its disease focus is inflammatory and autoimmune rather than cancer, with no tumour WGS or structural variant work.

entries.name: Flannick Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods that use human genetics to understand or treat disease, with a current emphasis on type 2 diabetes. Its main focus is calculating 'genetic support', meaning the likelihood that a given gene plays a role in a disease of interest. The methods are statistical and Bayesian. They model disease genetic architecture, integrate common- and rare-variant association data (including large exome sequencing datasets) with other omic data, and identify shared molecular causes across diseases with similar symptoms. The lab also coordinates the Knowledge Portal Network, which includes the Type 2 Diabetes Knowledge Portal, and serves as the Knowledge Center for the NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational and statistical genomics methods, but its work is germline human genetics of metabolic disease and data portals, not cancer, tumour sequencing, somatic or structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics. A US visa would also be needed.

entries.name: Hirschhorn Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses human genetics and genomics to find genes and variants that affect common diseases and traits, especially obesity and adult and childhood height (including the GIANT consortium). It runs large GWAS and meta-analyses, and rare-variant and exome analyses in biobank-scale cohorts. It develops computational methods to prioritise genes and variants and to extract biological insight from genetic data. Disease areas include pediatric skeletal growth, short stature, PCOS and reproductive endocrine disorders, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (HEDGE), and diabetic kidney disease. Work also combines genomic and metabolomic data.

fit.reason: There is some overlap in computational genomics methods, but the lab works on germline population genetics of height and obesity, with no cancer, somatic mutation, structural variant, tumour sequencing or single-cell/spatial work.

entries.name: Mercader Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses human genetics and genomics to find genetic variants associated with type 2 diabetes and related metabolic traits, with an emphasis on diverse ancestry populations. It characterizes how that genetic risk acts physiologically and molecularly, looking at specific large-effect variants and at people at the extremes of polygenic scores. Its methods include genome-wide association meta-analysis, whole-exome sequencing analysis, fine-mapping, polygenic risk scores, and re-analysis and integration of existing datasets. A further goal is translating these genetic findings to the clinic. This is population and statistical genetics of a metabolic disease, not cancer.

fit.reason: The lab shares computational genomics and statistical methods with the student, but it studies germline type 2 diabetes genetics rather than cancer, tumour WGS/transcriptome, somatic or structural variants, or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Lawrence Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses statistical and computational methods to study somatic DNA alterations in human genomes, including mutations and mutational processes. Its main topics are DNA damage and repair, the link between gene expression and genome replication, and the identification of cancer driver genes. Lawrence developed the MutSig suite, which finds significantly mutated genes against a heterogeneous mutational background in large cancer sequencing cohorts. The lab also analyzes mutational strand asymmetries to separate transcription-coupled from replication-coupled processes, and it has worked on APOBEC3A mutation signatures. It has built the TumorPortal resource, and the DrugMap atlas of cysteine ligandability across 416 cancer cell lines, with Liron Bar-Peled.

entries.name: Udler Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on diabetes precision diagnostics and management. It uses genetic data across the spectrum from rare to common variation to find new diabetes genes, subtypes and disease mechanisms. A major theme is clustering type 2 diabetes genetic loci into biological process-specific groups and polygenic scores, including a 2024 Nature Medicine study of more than 1.4 million people across ancestries. The group also leads MGH recruitment for the RADIANT study of atypical diabetes, which searches for rare variants. It analyses UK Biobank, Mass General Brigham Biobank, All of Us and the T2D Knowledge Portal, and it runs a clinical genetics program for monogenic diabetes.

fit.reason: The lab uses statistical and computational human genetics on biobank data, which overlaps loosely with the student's computational methods interest, but it has no cancer, tumour sequencing, somatic or structural variant, or single-cell/spatial work.

entries.name: Gehlenborg Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational and visualization techniques that let scientists and clinicians interact efficiently with large biomedical datasets. Past and current tools include HiGlass (web-based exploration of genome interaction maps and 3D genome conformation data) and UpSet (visualization of intersecting sets). The lab also works on visualization of heterogeneous cancer genomics data and on genomics and imaging tools for nucleome studies. Its postdoc openings include electronic health record visualization, and its members study how domain experts construct and explore genomics visualizations.

fit.reason: The lab builds visualization and interface tools, some for cancer genomics data, rather than doing sequencing-based discovery of structural variants or somatic mutations, so overlap with the student's interests is limited. It could suit collaboration or visualization tooling for their own data.

entries.name: Hacohen Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds systems-biology tools and models of immune processes to support personalized immunotherapy. It runs genome-wide genetic screens in primary immune cells, including work that identified STING as a proton channel. It also discovers immune cell types and states for the Human Cell Atlas, including dendritic cell subsets and T cell states, and links cell states to sepsis, lupus nephritis and cancer immunity. In cancer, it works on patient-specific neoantigen vaccines, using machine learning to predict antigens, and on spatially organized immune structures in tumours associated with effective immunotherapy. Several members use single-cell multimodal methods and deep learning.

fit.reason: There is solid overlap with the student's interests in single-cell and spatial omics in cancer and in machine learning for genomics, but the lab is immunology-centred rather than focused on tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis. It is also in the US, so a visa may be needed.

entries.name: Sabeti Lab
entries.focus: The Sabeti Lab develops genomic and computational tools to detect, track and contain infectious threats such as Ebola, Zika, Lassa, SARS-CoV-2 and malaria. Its work combines pathogen genomics, artificial intelligence, rapid diagnostics and outbreak intelligence. The lab also studies human genetics, building algorithms and molecular tools to find genetic and regulatory variation linked to health and disease, including natural selection in the human genome. It develops countermeasures such as diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines. It also builds outbreak-response capacity through programs such as Sentinel and the African Center of Excellence in Genomics of Infectious Disease, mainly in West Africa and the U.S.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's computational and machine-learning genomics methods, but its focus is infectious disease and human population genetics, with no cancer genomics, structural-variant or single-cell/spatial work found; a US visa would also likely be needed.

entries.name: Rigollet Lab
entries.focus: The group works on the mathematical foundations of statistics and machine learning. Current themes are Wasserstein gradient flows and statistical optimal transport, and transformers modelled as interacting particle systems, with self-attention treated as a velocity field. A biological strand applies optimal transport and transformers to populations of cells treated as probability measures. Earlier single-cell work includes Waddington-OT, which was developed with Broad collaborators to reconstruct developmental trajectories in reprogramming from scRNA-seq time courses.

fit.reason: The group's single-cell optimal-transport and ML methods touch the student's ML-for-genomics interest, but the work is mostly theoretical and has no cancer genomics, WGS or structural-variant analysis.

entries.name: Loh Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and computational methods for large-scale human genetics, using biobank-scale data such as the UK Biobank. A signature topic is detecting mosaic chromosomal alterations (clonal mosaicism) in blood-derived DNA from SNP-array data and studying their links to clonal haematopoiesis and disease risk. Related work includes mosaic copy-number variants (e.g. in autism), structural variation, and haplotype phasing and imputation. Other methods work targets the genetic architecture of complex traits and diseases.

fit.reason: The lab's mosaic and structural variant and somatic mutation methods overlap somewhat with the student's interests, but its focus is population-scale germline and biobank statistical genetics rather than cancer, tumour WGS/RNA-seq, or single-cell and spatial omics, and a US visa would be needed.

entries.name: Irizarry Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods and open-source software (largely R/Bioconductor) for interpreting large, noisy genomic and molecular datasets. Its work includes single-cell RNA-seq, such as technical variability and GLM-PCA dimensionality reduction. It also covers bulk RNA-seq quantification and normalization (Salmon, Alpine, CQN, DerFinder). DNA methylation work includes BSmooth, Bumphunter and minfi. Cross-cutting themes are normalization, batch-effect correction, and statistical modeling. Older work covers microarray and SNP-chip copy number analysis. The lab also does some public health and data science education work.

fit.reason: The lab's computational methods for single-cell and bulk transcriptomics overlap with the student's methods and single-cell interests, but it is not focused on cancer WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis. Roles in the US would also likely need a visa.

entries.name: Beroukhim Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how genetic changes during cancer evolution shape cancer behavior. The emphasis is on brain cancers, both adult and pediatric, and on chromosomal structural changes such as rearrangements and copy-number alterations across many cancer types. It has a longstanding effort in endometrial cancer, including clonal tracking of metastatic disease. Its methods are computational, built for large cancer genomic datasets, and include work on tumour evolution and on vulnerabilities linked to copy-number change. Some members add experimental work, for example on DNA-damage repair in pediatric gliomas.

fit.reason: The lab is strongly aligned with cancer genomics, structural variants, somatic copy-number analysis and computational methods, which are the student's core interests. Single-cell and spatial work is not obvious on the lab site, and a US visa would be needed.

entries.name: Xavier Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how human genetic variants regulate barrier defense and innate and adaptive immunity, with a focus on inflammatory bowel disease and the gut. It maps immune and metabolic states in the gut at single-cell resolution. It also studies how the microbiome affects health and disease, using human cohorts and computational models. It also develops computational methods to map pathway regulation during disease and treatment.

entries.name: Duan Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and machine-learning methods for biomedical data, especially electronic health records (EHR) and EHR-linked biobanks. Main topics are disease risk prediction models, detecting cross-phenotype association and pleiotropy in high-dimensional genetic data, and federated learning and meta-analysis for combining evidence across sites without sharing individual-level data. The lab also works on methods for imperfect real-world data, including missing data and measurement error. The work is mostly methodological biostatistics and statistical genetics, and I found no cancer-genomics or sequencing-specific focus on the PI's page.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational and machine-learning methods for genomics, but its work is EHR, biobank and federated-learning biostatistics, with no evident cancer WGS, structural-variant or single-cell/spatial work.

entries.name: Hormoz Lab
entries.focus: The lab asks how biological history shapes future cell fate. It combines experimental, theoretical, engineering and computational work to make those histories observable. Experimental threads include engineering cells to record lineage and signaling histories in their own DNA, barcoding cells and reading the barcodes in situ alongside transcriptomes, and long-term time-lapse imaging with mammalian mother machines. The lab also builds human gastruloid and organoid models of early development, including generating blood stem cells from ES cells. Computational and theory threads include differentiable models of development, population genetics and stochastic processes to reconstruct the origins of blood cancers, single-cell RNA-seq for bacteria, and directed viral evolution for gene delivery.
topics: blood cancer origins and population gene

entries.name: Naqvi Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies the quantitative control of gene expression in human development and the disease 'tipping points' that can result when expression falls outside a tolerated range. It centres on how transcription factors (TFs) ensure adequate and timely gene expression, which it studies through TF dosage changes. Its approach combines functional genomics (quantitative TF perturbations, multi-omic profiling, enhancer-usage mapping) with computational modeling. The experimental systems are stem cell-derived in vitro models of development. The lab calls its quantitative framework 'analog genomics'.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational and genomic methods, but it works on developmental gene regulation and TF dosage rather than cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutation, and it has no PhD students listed.

entries.name: Raychaudhuri Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and computational genetics methods to understand the genetic basis of autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. It integrates GWAS, fine-mapping and functional genomics (including eQTL and epigenomic data) to identify causal variants, genes and cell types. A large part of the work uses single-cell RNA-seq and related single-cell technologies, with methods for batch integration, cell-state mapping and disease-associated cell states in tissues such as synovium. It also studies HLA and immune-gene variation and runs consortium efforts (AMP AIM, IGVF, ITN, International RA Genetics Consortium). The focus is immune-mediated disease rather than cancer, and the group has few or no tumour sequencing or structural variant projects that I could verify.

fit.reason: Strong overlap in computational and machine learning methods and in single-cell omics, but the disease focus is autoimmunity and germline genetics, not cancer genomics, tumour WGS or somatic structural variants.

entries.name: McCarroll Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies human genetic variation and how it contributes to disease, with emphasis on schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Huntington's disease. It works on large-scale DNA rearrangements and structural variation, and on somatic mosaicism in neurons and peripheral tissues. Its methods include single-cell and single-nucleus genomics (Drop-Seq and related technologies), population-scale genetics and statistical analysis. Most projects combine experimental work with computational and statistical approaches. Current members also work on brain development and evolution, chromatin architecture, and neuron-glia transcriptomics.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps strongly on structural variants, somatic mutation and single-cell methods with a computational component, but its work is on brain and psychiatric disease rather than cancer genomics, and the lab is in the US, so a visa would be needed.

entries.focus: The lab studies how genetic variation leads to biological function, disease and prevention. It does this by combining whole-genome sequencing, multi-omics and phenotype data from population cohorts and biobanks with functional genomics experiments. They also cover variant functional annotation, causal inference (Mendelian randomization and mediation) and single-cell/spatial multiomic integration. The lab releases open tools such as FAVOR, STAAR and STAARpipeline.

They also include pattern formation and morphogenesis in synthetic biology, and neural-network-style molecular computation. The work is molecular programming and biophysics. It does not involve cancer genomics or sequencing data analysis.

entries.name: Purdom Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods for high-throughput genomic data. Its main current emphasis is single-cell RNA-seq from patient cohorts. This includes per-patient summary representations of scRNA-seq profiles, tests for comparing those profiles across populations, and benchmarking of batch-correction and integration methods (CZI Data Insights funding). Applied projects include single-cell biomarkers that distinguish skin rashes such as psoriasis and atopic dermatitis (with UCSF collaborators), and cortical neuron cell-type classification (NIH BRAIN Initiative). Past work includes analysis of tumour DNA-sequencing mutation spectra (with Raymond Cho and Paul Spellman) and multi-omic integration in sorghum drought response.

fit.reason: Methods work on single-cell data and machine learning is relevant, but the lab is statistics-first and its focus is single-cell and clinical (skin disease). Cancer genomics, WGS, structural variants and spatial omics are only touched on in past tumour-mutation work.

entries.focus: The lab develops technologies to probe genome structure and function, mapping where DNA-binding proteins sit along long, single DNA molecules with advanced DNA sequencing (the DiMeLo-seq approach is extended by lab members). A second major theme is the biology of centromeres, satellite DNA and heterochromatin, which are large tandemly repeated regions that are hard to study. The lab applies the new tools to understand how these regions are regulated and how they function in chromosome segregation. Its work is genome-biology and epigenomics oriented, not cancer-focused.

It uses AlphaFold structure-based analysis and embedding-based deep learning for sequence analysis.

A third area is single-cell genomics: clonal architecture, timing of somatic mutations, and mutation fitness estimated with mathematical modelling.

entries.name: Ewald Group
entries.focus: The group uses machine learning and multi-omics integration to find and characterise chemical hazards to humans and ecosystems. A main assay is image-based cell profiling (Cell Painting), which captures morphological changes in cells after chemical exposure. Current work includes the OASIS consortium, which screens about 1,500 liver-relevant compounds across liver cell models and organoids to predict liver toxicity. A collaboration with EMBL Heidelberg groups studies a pesticide library, and a fellowship project co-supervised with Mo Lotfollahi (Sanger) aims to predict cell morphology after exposure to 1,000 pesticides.

fit.reason: The lab shares computational and machine-learning methods with the student's interests, but it works on toxicology and cell imaging rather than cancer genomics, structural variants or tumour sequencing, and a UK role may need a visa.

entries.name: Lees Group
entries.focus: The lab studies how pathogenic bacteria evolve to become more pathogenic and transmissible. Its research areas are pangenome evolution, evolution across the whole bacterial domain, and bacterial population genomics. Examples include post-vaccine selection in S. pneumoniae, speciation in Neisseria and Haemophilus, and capsule evolution. It builds evolutionary bioinformatics and modelling software (the bacpop tools on GitHub) that runs in a browser, on a laptop, or on GPUs. It uses machine learning, Bayesian models, dN/dS selection methods, bacterial GWAS and pangenome graphs. It also co-runs the AllTheBacteria resource. This is microbial rather than cancer genomics.

fit.reason: The overlap is limited to computational methods and machine learning for genomics, and to large-scale sequence analysis; the lab works on bacterial evolution and has no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variant or single-cell/spatial work. A UK role would also need a visa.

entries.name: Saez-Rodriguez Group
entries.focus: The group works in systems biomedicine. It studies how cellular signalling and regulatory networks become deregulated in disease, and it uses that knowledge to guide therapeutics. Disease areas are cancer, autoimmune disease and fibrotic disease, especially in kidney, heart and liver. Methods combine large-scale omics (including single-cell data) with mechanistic prior knowledge, using statistical and machine learning approaches. The group releases open-source software tools and supports DREAM crowdsourcing challenges.

fit.reason: The group overlaps on computational/ML methods and single-cell omics in cancer, but it centres on network modelling and functional/pathway inference. It does little on tumour WGS or structural variant calling, and a UK role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Goldman Group
entries.focus: The group develops mathematical, statistical and computational methods for analysing genome data. Its aim is to infer the processes that produced the data and to predict the biology encoded in genomes. The work covers new evolutionary models and methods, software and web services that make them available to other scientists, and applied comparative genomics and next-generation sequencing data analysis. The group also helped establish DNA data storage, which uses DNA to archive digital information.

fit.reason: The lab's computational and statistical genomics methods overlap loosely with the student's interest in computational methods, but I found no focus on cancer genomics, structural variants, somatic mutation, or single-cell or spatial omics. The lab is also in the UK, which may require a visa.

entries.name: Finn Group (Microbiome Informatics)
entries.focus: The group studies whole microbiomes, including the understudied viral and eukaryotic (single-cell) fractions, to understand how microbial communities function and interact. It examines how mobile genetic elements generate genomic diversity, including in opportunistic pathogens and drug-resistant microbes. It adopts long-read sequencing to capture microbial diversity and recover high-quality genomes from low-yield environments. The long-term aim is to understand the role of microbial communities in health and disease, including in under-represented geographic populations, and to support applications such as pathogen surveillance. The team also builds the MGnify resource and maintains the HMMER web server.

fit.reason: The work is microbiome and metagenomics infrastructure, with essentially no overlap with cancer genomics, tumour WGS/transcriptome, structural variants, or single-cell/spatial cancer omics beyond a general computational-genomics flavour; a UK role would also need a visa.

entries.name: Keane Group (visiting)
entries.focus: The group does computational comparative genomics, mainly in mouse and other rodents. It studies the structure, function and gene regulation of the most diverse loci in the mouse genome, including strain-specific diversity regions (SSDRs). These regions are enriched for genes involved in immunity, sensory functions, sexual reproduction and behaviour. It produces reference-quality genome assemblies for 16 mouse strains as part of the Mouse Genomes Project. It also sequences other rodents, such as spiny mice (Acomys) and the Algerian mouse, that are relevant to biomedicine and climate. The PI also leads strategic planning for the EGA and EVA data archives and co-leads the GA4GH Large-scale Genomics workstream.

fit.reason: There is some overlap through structural variants, genome analysis methods and the EGA archive for human genomic data, but the group works on rodent comparative genomics. It does not work on cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, or single-cell or spatial omics.

entries.name: Coorens Group
entries.focus: The group develops computational tools for somatic mutation data. These include mutation calling and phylogenetic tree reconstruction, which use somatic mutations as lineage barcodes to trace cell ancestry. They compare mutation rates, mutational processes and cancer-driver genes across normal human tissues, and study how lifestyle, exposures and inflammation shape them. They also build large phylogenies of normal cells to study early embryogenesis and the origins of childhood cancers, by comparing cancer and normal cell lineages. The group is part of the NIH-funded SMaHT Network and the dGTEx Consortium.

fit.reason: Strong overlap on somatic mutation analysis and computational genomics methods, but the focus is mostly normal-tissue mosaicism and lineage tracing rather than tumour WGS, structural variants, transcriptomics or single-cell/spatial omics, and a UK role may need a visa.

entries.name: Uhlmann Group (visiting)
entries.focus: The group develops methods to quantify morphology from microscopy images in 2D, 3D, static and dynamic data across imaging modalities. It extracts geometric shape models from images with minimal manual input. It then treats collections of shapes as distributions to compare and characterize them, and to generate synthetic shapes. Methods draw on approximation theory, machine learning and computational geometry. The group applies them to biological discovery, often with experimental collaborators. Related work includes the Fractal platform for large-scale bioimage analysis.

fit.reason: The group has a strong computational and machine-learning methods flavour, but it works on microscopy image morphology rather than cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, so overlap is limited.

entries.name: Dynamics of Living Systems Laboratory
entries.focus: The lab studies how cells respond to changes in their environment. It combines experiments with computer modelling to find the basic rules by which cells organise themselves and function. The computational work builds mechanistic models from known biology and extends them with machine learning to find new patterns in data. The experimental side uses automated lab techniques and high-throughput assays to measure single-cell responses to many treatments at scale. A past job posting described work on the regulatory 'grammar' of phosphorylation dynamics and on cell cycle dynamics inferred from snapshot mass cytometry data.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in computational and machine-learning methods and single-cell data, but it works on signalling and cell-state dynamics and does not focus on cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variants or somatic mutations.

entries.name: Developmental Dynamics Laboratory
entries.focus: The lab studies how gene regulatory networks and morphogen signalling (Shh, BMP, Wnt) specify cell fates and pattern tissue, using the vertebrate neural tube and spinal cord as the main model. Its research areas include gene regulation, developmental tempo, growth and lineage, stem cells and bioengineering, and computational approaches. Methods include single-cell and lineage analysis, optogenetics, chromatin and epigenetic profiling, stem-cell-derived tissue models, and comparative work in chick, mouse, human and marsupial systems. A substantial computational arm develops machine learning, mathematical modelling and information-theoretic methods to infer gene regulatory logic from genome sequence and single-cell data. The work is developmental biology, not cancer.

fit.reason: There is overlap in computational and ML methods for single-cell and regulatory genomics (e.g. Kleshchevnikov, Volteras, Radley), but the lab works on developmental biology with no cancer genomics, tumour WGS or structural variant focus, and it is in the UK, which may mean a visa.

entries.name: Bioinformatics and Computational Biology Laboratory
entries.focus: The unit combines computational and experimental methods to study gene regulation, genome evolution and population genomics. Its main model is the marine zooplankton Oikopleura dioica, a larvacean. Topics include comparative genomics of O. dioica (cryptic speciation, gene-order evolution), population genomics and pangenomics of Ryukyu Islands populations, and marine climate-change adaptation through temperature, pH and salinity stress experiments. Other topics are functional genomics (epigenetic and transcriptional regulation) and development of a new de novo genome assembly algorithm. Student projects also include cryo-EM/cryo-ET of the larvacean house and bioluminescence. Cancer work is not part of the unit's current listed topics.

fit.reason: The computational genomics and genome-assembly methods overlap loosely with the student's interest in methods, but the unit works on marine zooplankton rather than cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial cancer omics, and the move to Japan adds a relocation hurdle.

entries.name: Cancer Dynamics Laboratory
entries.focus: The lab uses evolutionary biology to study why individual cancers follow different courses, especially how metastases and drug resistance emerge. It concentrates on renal cell carcinoma (clear cell RCC) and melanoma. The group is made up of cancer geneticists, computational biologists and clinician scientists. Its methods include multi-omics analysis of patient samples, patient-derived organoid models of ccRCC evolution, studies of the immune microenvironment, and mathematical simulation of tumour evolution. A related collaboration with MD Anderson looks at diet, obesity and kidney cancer.

entries.focus: The Sunyaev Lab is a computational genomics group that studies genetic variation. This covers how mutations arise and evolve, how variants change molecular function and structure, and how population genetics shapes evolution. It also has cancer genomics projects, including tumorigenesis and progression modeling co-advised with the Van Allen lab.

entries.name: Keating Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies protein-protein interactions in eukaryotic signaling and human health. It also builds molecules that selectively disrupt or modulate those interactions. A major thread is the Bcl-2 family of apoptosis regulators. Structure-based and machine-learning models predict how BH3-motif helices bind the anti-apoptotic family members. Newer projects look at short linear motif (SLiM) binding by TRAF and EVH1 domains and at the E3 ligase Itch. Methods include computational protein and peptide design, ML models of sequence-structure-energy landscapes, yeast surface display, and photo-crosslinking of peptide interactions.

entries.focus: The lab studies Mycobacterium tuberculosis, including why infection outcomes differ between individuals and what drives lesions toward bacterial clearance. The long-term goal is to inform a TB vaccine.

entries.focus: The group develops theory, methods and algorithms for probabilistic graphical models and causal inference. It draws on algebraic geometry, combinatorics, convex optimization, statistics and machine learning. entries.name: Burge Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how genes are expressed and regulated, combining computational and experimental methods. Its main topics are the rules that define introns and splice sites, splicing enhancer and repressor motifs that are tested in vivo, and alternative splicing as a regulatory mechanism in vertebrates. It also develops algorithms for gene identification in eukaryotic genomes and for finding microRNAs and predicting their functions. Recent lab papers cover LUC7 splicing regulators (Kenny et al., 2025), random introns (Kowal et al., 2025) and KATMAP, a splicing-factor activity model (McGurk et al., 2024 preprint).

fit.reason: The lab is computational and transcriptome-focused, which overlaps somewhat with the student's methods interests. It is centred on RNA processing and splicing biology rather than cancer genomics, structural variants, somatic mutations or single-cell/spatial omics. It would also need a US visa.

entries.name: Computational Biophysics Group
entries.focus: The group's work has moved mainly to machine learning for clinical decision making. Its signal-processing and ML models build cardiovascular risk biomarkers by combining clinical history, genetic information and physiologic signals such as echocardiograms and EHR time series. Current student work covers contrastive and representation learning on multimodal clinical data, and the robustness, fairness and trustworthiness of ML in healthcare. The group's original line of work is computational molecular biophysics. It models conformational changes and the unfolded ensembles of disordered proteins linked to neurodegeneration, such as tau, alpha-synuclein and amyloid-beta.

entries.focus: The lab studies genetic differences between males and females, in the reproductive tract and throughout the body, and how those differences affect biology and medicine. entries.focus: The lab analyzes and designs genetic networks, from fully synthetic circuits to circuits that interact with a cell's own regulatory networks. A main theme is the context-dependence of genetic circuits, such as resource loading and retroactivity. The lab uses feedback control design and dynamical-systems modelling to reduce that dependence. A key application is engineering circuits that control cell-fate transitions for regenerative medicine, such as reprogramming. The work combines control theory, mathematical modelling and wet-lab synthetic biology in mammalian and bacterial cells.

entries.name: Mirny Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses polymer physics, biophysical modelling and genomic data analysis to study how chromosomes are folded in 3D and how that folding affects gene regulation. A major theme is loop extrusion by cohesin and condensin, including the kinetics of cohesin-mediated contacts, enhancer-promoter communication, and sister-chromatid organization. Other themes are epigenetic memory and cell-fate maintenance, nuclear organization and mechanics, and the role of non-coding RNAs in chromatin structure. Methods include Hi-C and other chromosome-conformation data analysis, Bayesian inference, machine-learning tools, and simulations. The lab also has work on evolutionary and computational biology, and some past work on cancer genomics and evolution.

entries.name: Blainey Lab
entries.focus: The lab combines microfluidics, molecular biology and optics to build new measurement methods for biology. Its main current project is pooled optical genetic screening. CRISPR perturbations are identified by in situ sequencing and linked to image-based phenotypes across millions of human cells, including a map of the phenotypic landscape of essential genes. A second area is scalable droplet-based combinatorial screening, for example drug combinations that re-sensitize Gram-negative bacteria to antibiotics. A third is single-cell genomics, covering virtual microfluidics and enrichment of rare cells in pooled scRNA-seq. A fourth is a 'somatic mutation flow' method that analyzes mutations jointly across cells linked by lineage, with relevance to aging and cancer.

entries.name: Greener Group (biomolecular simulation / force fields)
entries.focus: The group works on improving the force fields used for biomolecular simulation. One approach trains fast molecular mechanics force fields with graph neural networks, using quantum mechanics and experimental data. The aim is a reproducible, universal model that covers the molecules found in biology. A second approach develops faster machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for biomolecules, using simpler models and GPU programming. The long-term goal is to simulate enzyme reactions. The motivation is that current force fields can be inaccurate, for example for disordered proteins and protein aggregation. This work connects to differentiable simulation and to understanding aggregated proteins in neurodegenerative disease.

entries.focus: The lab studies the chromosomal structure of DNA in cancer. It uses cancer genome assembly and long-molecule sequencing, including Pore-C, to resolve complex somatic rearrangements. It develops new algorithms and genomic assays and applies them to clinical samples. A central question is how complex structural variants shape the tumour epigenome, and the reverse. Structural variation is also used to study the mutational processes behind somatic evolution, from pre-cancer to metastasis. The long-term aim is genomic diagnostics and precision cancer care.

entries.name: Wall Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops biomedical informatics and systems biology methods for conditions that begin in childhood, especially autism and related developmental delays. A major strand is digital diagnostics and therapeutics: machine learning on home video and mobile data for autism detection, and wearable-based (Autism Glass) therapy. A second strand uses genomic data from autism cohorts such as iHART to find gene-disease associations in mental disorders, and builds computational and bioinformatics software for this. The work is mostly clinical ML, computer vision and human-centred AI. It is not oncology.

entries.name: Stanford Translational AI (STAI) Lab

The data are mostly neuroimaging, video and wearable or ambient sensing, and the lab does not appear to work on genomics.

entries.name: Lundberg Lab
entries.focus: The lab works in spatial proteomics and cell biology. It combines bioimaging, proteomics and AI to map how human proteins are distributed in space and time inside cells. A long-term goal is the first spatiotemporal proteome model of a human cell, built with machine learning on imaging data plus other data types, including multi-scale cell models, 'digital twin' perturbation models and foundation models. The lab produces the Subcellular Section of the Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas and develops highly multiplexed immunofluorescence, Deep Visual Proteomics (laser microdissection plus mass spectrometry) and subcellular RNA localization methods. It also studies single-cell protein variation, primary cilia and mislocalization in disease, and runs crowd-sourced open-science challenges.

fit.reason: Overlap is limited to ML methods for genomics and some spatial/single-cell omics (with a few cancer-tissue imaging projects), while the lab is proteomics/imaging-centred and does no tumour WGS, structural variant or somatic mutation work.

entries.name: Ashley Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on precision medicine. It develops methods to interpret whole-genome sequencing data for diagnosing rare and undiagnosed genetic disease, including ultra-rapid genomic diagnosis. It applies AI and deep learning at several scales, including multimodal cardiovascular risk prediction, ECG, echo and MRI models, and deep-learning variant interpretation. Digital health and exercise-physiology work includes the My Heart Counts study, wearables, and MoTrPAC multi-omics. Wet-lab and translational projects cover cardiomyopathy genetics, genome editing, and gene therapy and non-viral delivery to cardiomyocytes.

fit.reason: Genome-sequencing and ML methods overlap somewhat with the student's computational genomics interests, but the lab's focus is cardiovascular and rare germline disease, with little cancer, somatic-mutation, structural-variant or single-cell/spatial work.

entries.focus: The lab trains and evaluates foundation models for healthcare, working where computer science, medical informatics and hospital systems meet. entries.name: Huang Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how bacterial cells control their shape, size and internal organization, including the cytoskeleton (MreB), cell wall and envelope mechanics, and how these respond to antibiotics, osmolarity and temperature. entries.name: Steinmetz Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how genetic variation shapes molecular and cellular traits and disease. entries.name: Gevaert Lab
entries.focus: The lab works on biomedical data fusion: machine learning methods that integrate multi-scale data (molecular omics, cellular-level pathology and tissue-level medical imaging) for clinical decision support. Its main application areas are oncology and neuroscience, including brain cancer. Earlier work used Bayesian and kernel methods on breast and ovarian cancer data and developed algorithms that identify driver genes from multi-omics data. Current projects include histology-genomic integration, deep learning for digital pathology, and epigenomic and transcriptomic biomarker discovery.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps on cancer omics and machine learning for genomics, but its emphasis is on imaging, pathology and multimodal fusion rather than whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or single-cell and spatial omics, and a US role may need a visa.

entries.name: Daneshjou Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops and evaluates machine learning and AI methods for biomedicine and healthcare, with an emphasis on rigor and fairness. A third is dermatology research: building datasets that cover diverse skin tones, predicting outcomes, finding biomarkers and analysing images. The lab also works on bias, AI regulation and reporting standards.

entries.focus: The lab studies somatic evolution in cancer. It looks at how mutational processes shape cell plasticity and stress adaptation, and how tumour cells interact with their microenvironment to resist therapy and persist in tissue. It builds statistical, data-integration and machine learning methods that link bulk genomics, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and digital pathology. A UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship supports work on the mutational processes and spatial context of tumour dormancy. The group works on genomic instability and tumour-immune crosstalk during cancer progression.

entries.name: Computational Cancer Genomics (CCG) Group
entries.focus: The group designs and applies computational methods to tumour DNA sequencing data, mainly single-cell whole-genome data, to study cancer evolution and metastasis. They build probabilistic tumour phylogenies that combine SNVs, copy-number changes and structural variants, and report several equally plausible solutions. Further work covers the fraction of replicating cells per subpopulation (SPRINTER), replication-timing alterations as non-genetic drivers, metastatic migration patterns, and the use of mutational signatures as molecular clocks to time metastatic seeding. They also analyse bulk sequencing from the TRACERx lung cancer cohort (842 patients), and prostate cancer autopsy and glioblastoma datasets with collaborators.

fit.reason: Strong overlap on cancer genomics, structural variants and somatic mutation analysis, computational methods, and single-cell sequencing; less emphasis on transcriptome or spatial omics and on machine learning, and a UK role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Yang group (molecular evolution, phylogenetics); Director, UCL Centre for Computational Biology
entries.focus: The lab develops maximum likelihood and Bayesian statistical methods for comparative analysis of molecular sequence data. Its main topics are phylogenetics, molecular clock dating and species delimitation, along with the detection of positive selection. Its software includes PAML for phylogenetic analysis by maximum likelihood, and BPP for Bayesian multispecies-coalescent analysis. It also builds MCMC algorithms that scale to large genomic datasets, and Bayesian relaxed-clock dating. The lab describes itself as a small, collaborative group with backgrounds in evolutionary genetics, genomics, computer science and statistics.

It does no cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variant analysis or single-cell/spatial omics. A move to the UK would also probably need a visa.

entries.name: Comparative Somatic Evolutionary Genomics
entries.focus: The group studies how somatic mutations accumulate in normal cells over a lifetime and form clonal expansions that may drive cancer and ageing. They use laser capture microdissection and low-input and duplex sequencing to measure somatic mutation burdens and mutational signatures in normal tissues. The comparative approach spans many species, including non-human primates, other mammals and plants. Three themes run through the work: ageing, cancer resistance across species (Peto's paradox), and using pollutant-linked mutational signatures in sentinel species for environmental monitoring. A Wellcome grant covers somatic mutation and clonal dynamics across about 30 species.

fit.reason: The group overlaps on somatic mutation analysis, mutational signatures and sequencing-based computational methods. It studies normal tissue across species rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and a UK role would need a visa.

entries.name: Computational Biology of DNA Replication and Repair
entries.focus: The lab is a computational biology group that studies how cells replicate and repair DNA, with an emphasis on replication stress. Replication stress is when forks slow or stall, and it can cause genomic instability. They build high-performance mathematical modelling methods and AI models to analyse large genomic sequencing datasets. They package these as scalable, easy-to-use software. A well-known example is D-NAscent, which detects BrdU on nanopore reads to map replication fork movement on single molecules. The work also asks whether replication errors can be exploited therapeutically in human cancer cells and parasites.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps on computational and ML methods for genomics and on cancer genomic instability. Its focus is replication dynamics from nanopore data, not tumour WGS/transcriptome analysis, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and the student would need a UK visa.

entries.name: Large-scale evolutionary inference
entries.focus: The group develops statistical and computational phylogenetics methods that scale to millions of closely related genomes. This is based on the group's published tools, not a lab description. The Cambridge pages I could read give no research description. Published tools include MAPLE, a fast maximum-likelihood phylogenetic inference method for pandemic-scale SARS-CoV-2 and bacterial genome collections. They also include SPRTA, which gives confidence scores for branches of very large trees, and the simulators phastSim and VGsim. The work targets genomic epidemiology and evolutionary inference. The main inputs are viral and bacterial genomes, not tumour sequencing.

fit.reason: The group is strong on scalable computational methods for genomics. It works on pathogen phylogenetics, not cancer genomics, structural variants, tumour sequencing, or single-cell and spatial omics, so topical overlap with the student is small.

entries.name: Creixell Group (Cancer signalling and therapeutics)
entries.focus: The lab combines machine learning with high-throughput biochemistry to study how proteins, especially protein kinases, recognise their substrates. It asks how this recognition goes wrong in cancer, with an emphasis on oncogenic drivers in brain tumours. It also asks how it can be used to design selective, mutant-specific drugs that overcome resistance. The lab website lists three areas: Cancer Signalling, Cancer Resistance & Therapeutics, and Protein Design & Engineering. Current student projects include computational protein and nanobody design against phosphorylation-dependent epitopes, protein-protein interaction-based therapeutics, kinase signalling in CML, and kinase inhibitor screening for glioblastoma.

fit.reason: The lab applies ML and computational design to protein biochemistry, kinase signalling and therapeutics. It does not do cancer genomics, WGS or transcriptome analysis, structural variants or single-cell and spatial omics, so only the general computational and ML interest overlaps.

entries.name: Computational evolution of development in plants
entries.focus: The group studies the evolutionary dynamics of developmental processes, mainly in plants, using an evolutionary developmental biology (evo-devo) approach. It builds mathematical and computational models that simulate evolving populations over millions of years. These show how mutations can produce new developmental programs and organs such as branches, roots and leaves. A major theme is the evolution of the apical stem cell niche (shoot apical meristem). Models use gene regulatory networks and pattern formation, and the group collaborates with modelling and experimental labs at the Sainsbury Laboratory and elsewhere in Cambridge.

fit.reason: The group does theoretical evolutionary modelling of plant development, with no cancer genomics, sequencing data, structural variant analysis or single-cell/spatial omics. The only overlap is general computational biology.

entries.name: Computational Physics of Chromatin
entries.focus: The group builds multiscale computational models of chromatin to explain how the genome is organised in 3D at the nanoscale. Their models draw on all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, coarse-graining methods and theory. They also use experimental data from collaborators. A central aim is to link epigenomic states to the chromatin nanostructures they produce, and to identify the molecular mechanisms behind those links. This is physics-based biophysics of chromatin, not sequencing-data analysis.

fit.reason: The group does physics-based simulation of chromatin structure, with little overlap with cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants, genomics ML or single-cell/spatial omics, and a UK role would need a visa.

entries.name: Teichmann Group
entries.focus: The lab co-founded and co-leads the Human Cell Atlas. It uses single-cell and spatial genomics to map the cell composition of healthy and diseased human tissues. A major theme is human immunology: immune development (including in the thymus and during pregnancy), tissue-resident and cross-tissue immune cells, and T cell responses. The lab also develops technology and computational methods, such as the CellPhoneDB cell-cell communication tool and the CellTypist annotation tool, along with batch correction and AI approaches for single-cell and spatial data. Roughly half of the group works in dry-lab roles, and organoids are used for functional validation. Cancer-related work is limited, e.g. anti-cancer immunity in organoids and spatial organization in glioma.

fit.reason: The lab is very strong in single-cell and spatial omics and in computational and ML methods, but it focuses on immunology and cell atlases rather than cancer genomics, tumour WGS or structural variants, and the UK location may require a visa.

entries.focus: The lab uses mathematical and statistical models of infectious disease transmission. It combines these with pathogen genomic data and large-scale mobile phone and satellite data. A major focus is the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, at both the within-host and population levels. This includes how human mobility and labour migration spread malaria and drug-resistant parasites. The group also works on dengue and on predicting and containing the spatial spread of emerging epidemics, and it supports national malaria control programmes with surveillance and analytical approaches for targeting interventions. It co-leads the COVID-19 Mobility Data Network. The work is population-level epidemiology and modelling, not tumour or cancer genomics.

entries.name: Trynka Group
entries.focus: The group studies how genetic variation shapes immune cell function and contributes to immune-mediated disease. One approach is single-cell eQTL mapping in resting and stimulated immune cells. This includes Project JAGUAR, which looks at how genetic ancestry and admixture shape immune gene regulation in Latin American populations. A second approach is CRISPR perturbation, including single-cell CRISPR screens, of disease-associated genes in primary human T cells. A third is high-content imaging of cell morphology and function. They combine these with computational and statistical genetics to turn GWAS variants into target genes and candidate therapeutic targets.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and single-cell genomics methods, but its focus is germline variants and immune disease rather than cancer, tumour WGS or somatic and structural variants, and it has no spatial omics work.

entries.name: Meier Group
entries.focus: The group studies how interbreeding (hybridisation) and chromosomal rearrangements drive rapid speciation and adaptation. Its systems include Lake Victoria cichlid fishes, Neotropical Ithomiini and Heliconius butterflies, cribellate spiders, wall lizards and ladybird beetles. Methods are population genomics, comparative genomics across lineages, transcriptomics, and single-cell sequencing of butterfly sperm to measure recombination. Current projects ask why some Lepidoptera have heavily rearranged chromosomes, how rearrangements affect gene flow and speciation rate, and how traits evolve or are lost.

fit.reason: The group's work on structural variants, chromosome rearrangements and computational genomics overlaps methodologically with the student's interests, but it is evolutionary genomics in non-model organisms, with no cancer, tumour sequencing, somatic mutation or spatial omics.

entries.name: Google DeepMind
entries.focus: DeepMind's science teams build foundation models for biology. AlphaFold predicts protein structures, and its database holds more than 200 million predictions that researchers can still use. AlphaGenome takes up to 1 Mb of DNA sequence and predicts regulatory-variant effects at single-nucleotide resolution, covering gene expression, splicing, chromatin accessibility and related readouts. This makes it directly relevant to interpreting non-coding somatic and germline variants. Model weights and an API are available for non-commercial research. DeepMind has also opened PhD student researcher roles on cancer discovery. Press reports from July 2026 say the dedicated AlphaFold team was broken up and its staff reassigned to Gemini-based 'AI co-scientist' systems, genomics and other areas. John Jumper and some colleagues reportedly left for Anthropic.

fit.reason: AlphaGenome and the cancer-discovery work overlap strongly with variant interpretation, ML for genomics and cancer genomics. Single-cell and spatial omics and SV analysis are less central, and programs are competitive, US/UK-based and need work authorization.

Prescient Design's own work is mainly molecule design, not tumour genomics.

entries.name: GRAIL
entries.focus: GRAIL develops multi-cancer early detection tests. Its main product is Galleri, a blood test that finds a cancer signal and predicts where in the body it started. The test reads cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation patterns, using targeted sequencing and machine-learning classifiers trained on large clinical cohorts. The Computational Biology and Machine Learning (CBML) group builds the diagnostic classifiers. It also does bioinformatics on large genomic datasets and develops methods for post-diagnostic applications. Cancer genomics is central to the work. Programs include large prospective studies such as NHS-Galleri and PATHFINDER.

fit.reason: Strong overlap in cancer genomics and ML for sequencing data. However, the work centres on cfDNA methylation, not tumour WGS, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and the programs are US-based with no open student roles.

entries.name: Foundation Medicine
entries.focus: Foundation Medicine runs comprehensive genomic profiling tests for cancer (FoundationOne CDx, FoundationOne Liquid CDx and heme assays). The tests detect somatic variants, copy-number changes, rearrangements and fusions, and genomic signatures such as TMB and MSI in tumour tissue and blood. The computational discovery and computational biology groups analyse its large clinico-genomic database to find biomarkers and new genomic signatures. They also develop algorithms and take them from discovery into validated clinical products, and they support pharma partners with companion diagnostics and real-world evidence. The work centres on targeted DNA/RNA sequencing and clinical-grade bioinformatics, not research whole-genome or single-cell work.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with cancer genomics, somatic mutation and structural variant analysis, and computational methods. It has little WGS, transcriptome, single-cell or spatial work, and US work authorization is a hurdle.
